items.t: Hermès Heir Seeking €14 Billion Over Missing Shares Faces Mental Capacity Scrutiny
sum: A Swiss lawyer under investigation over the disappearance of an Hermès heir’s shares is challenging a judicial order to assess the heir’s cognitive capacity, a procedural dispute that could influence the criminal case behind a €14 billion civil damages claim.

Alexandre Montavon, who previously advised LVMH during its accumulation of Hermès shares, has appealed the examination order, Reuters reported, citing two people with direct knowledge of the decision.
The Paris judge then ordered psychiatrists to assess 83-year-old Nicolas Puech.

The dispute matters because French criminal law separately penalizes exploitation of a person whose vulnerability is apparent or known to the offender. Under the law, the offense carries up to three years in prison and a €375,000 fine in its basic form.

Montavon was placed under formal investigation in May on suspicion of complicity in breach of trust. Prosecutors suspect him of participating in the alleged diversion of Puech’s shares for LVMH’s benefit. He denies wrongdoing.
Puech maintains that he discovered in 2022 that his approximately 6% holding in Hermès had disappeared after entrusting his finances to Swiss wealth manager Eric Freymond for more than two decades.

He is pursuing €14 billion in damages from defendants including LVMH and its chairman, Bernard Arnault. Reuters estimates the missing shares’ current value at approximately $9 billion, separate from the damages being sought.

items.t: Hermès International stock faces China drag as leather goods hold up
sum: Hermès International's third-quarter performance exposed a sharper divide between its core leather business and adjacent luxury categories. In a report published Wednesday, November 11, ad-hoc-news.de, citing Reuters, said currency-adjusted third-quarter sales rose 4.3 percent year on year to 4.10 billion euros, below the 5.2 percent analyst expectation.

Leather goods, including the Birkin and Kelly handbag franchises, delivered the strongest support. Sales in the division increased 10.8 percent from a year earlier, highlighting continued demand for Hermès products with tightly controlled supply and strong pricing power.

The wider portfolio was less resilient. Ready-to-wear and accessories sales fell 2 percent year on year, reversing several years of growth. Finance chief Eric du Halgouet attributed the contraction to weak Chinese demand, while the division continued to grow in other regions.

Management described the Chinese market as very difficult but maintained confidence in its long-term prospects and plans to keep investing there. The company also retained its plan to increase total production volumes by about 6 percent in the coming years.

For investors, the key question is whether leather goods can continue to offset weaker demand in watches, beauty and other categories. A prolonged slowdown in China would test the breadth of Hermès' growth even if its flagship handbag business remains strong.

sum: LVMH shares climbed 7.0% over seven days, a move that media reports tied to a broader recovery across the luxury sector rather than to anything happening inside the company itself. The advance stretched across four consecutive trading sessions and coincided with a pickup in European equity indices.

Behind the run, according to those reports, was a rotation out of AI-linked stocks. Investors also latched onto hopes that the US midterm elections could usher in less turbulent international relations — a shift that would presumably ease conditions for trade and tourism. Both tailwinds lifted the sector as a whole; neither reflected a company-specific development at LVMH.

The rotation came even as LVMH was busy promoting the technology investors were moving away from. On Tuesday the group hosted the third instalment of its "Business of Tomorrow" series in Paris, drawing close to 350 attendees, with applications of artificial intelligence across its various business lines as the centrepiece.

On the same day, LVMH lodged a notification with the French financial markets authority, the AMF, covering share transactions between 26 and 30 October. The filing detailed purchases under the group's approved buyback programme, which was authorised on 23 April. LVMH bought 50,000 of its own shares on each trading day of that window, with the stated aim of cancelling them. For further particulars, the company pointed to its regulated information section.

At Louis Vuitton, Hector Muelas took over the newly created position of Chief Brand Creative Officer on 1 November, according to media reports. The appointment, announced on 23 October, covers creative brand communications, campaigns and content production — essentially the tasks surrounding how the maison presents and communicates itself.

Operationally, LVMH reported revenue of EUR 57.1 billion for the first nine months of 2026 on 12 October, with organic growth of 2%. The fashion and leather goods division, however, saw organic revenue fall 5% in the third quarter of 2026.

Away from the trading floor, the group's Institut des Métiers d'Excellence recorded a completion rate of 91% for one of its cohorts, and has trained more than 4,300 apprentices through the programme since 2014.

LVMH Discloses 494.6 Million Shares as Zenith Weighs Swiss Job Cuts
sum: LVMH has laid out its capital structure as of 31 October, reporting 494,606,080 outstanding shares in a regulatory disclosure. The filing puts gross voting rights at 743,358,184 and net voting rights at 739,382,278 — three separate figures that describe different facets of the group's ownership base. The notice is a snapshot at a fixed date, not a signal of any new transaction.

That distinction matters, because the disclosure lands alongside two unrelated developments at the French luxury giant: a repositioning at its watch brand Zenith and a French judicial review of the group's historical Hermès stake.

Zenith confirmed on 23 October that it will pivot toward higher-end timepieces and lower production volumes. The LVMH-owned brand simultaneously opened an employee consultation on the plan. According to media reports, as many as half of its Swiss workforce could be affected by job cuts.

No final decision on redundancies is expected before the consultation closes on 12 November, meaning the potential staff reductions remain undecided. The strategic shift itself, by contrast, has already been confirmed by the brand.

French investigators are also examining LVMH's role in the acquisition of Hermès shares. As Le Monde reported on 30 October, the probe into the vanished shares of Hermès heir Nicolas Puech has shifted its focus to that question. The investigating magistrate reportedly plans to summon Bernard Arnault — a reported procedural step in an ongoing inquiry, not a finding of wrongdoing.

The judge has also questioned LVMH executive Jean-Jacques Guiony about the historical purchase of a 17% stake in Hermès, linked to Puech's missing shares. LVMH has said it will not comment on pending proceedings. The scrutiny concerns the group's past stake-building in a rival, not its own shares covered by today's disclosure — and the filing offers no answer to those legal questions.

LVMH shares slipped 1.2% yesterday. On the corporate calendar, the Zenith consultation wraps up on 12 November, and the group's Nona Source platform — which reuses luxury materials — holds a sale in Paris from 24 to 28 November, a part of the business distinct from the watch brand's overhaul.

sum: Hermès reported revenue of 12.3 billion euros for the first nine months of 2026, up 6 percent at constant exchange rates and 3 percent at current exchange rates from the same period a year earlier. The update, published on October 27, shows that the French luxury group continues to expand, although regional and category trends remain uneven.

The figures were reported by World Footwear. Third-quarter revenue reached 4.1 billion euros, rising 4 percent at constant exchange rates and 6 percent at current exchange rates. The quarter matched the second quarter in reported revenue, pointing to continued expansion but less even momentum across the portfolio.

Leather goods and saddlery delivered the strongest performance in the nine-month period, with sales up 10 percent at constant exchange rates. Silk and textiles grew 7 percent, while the group’s other activities, including jewelry and home products, increased 3 percent.

Other categories were weaker. Ready-to-wear and accessories advanced 1 percent, while perfume and beauty declined 1 percent. Watches fell 2 percent, making it one of the group’s weakest areas alongside beauty. The contrast leaves Hermès more dependent on the resilience of its core leather business as customers remain selective in discretionary spending.

The Americas led regional growth with a 13 percent increase at constant exchange rates. Japan followed with 11 percent growth, while Europe excluding France rose 9 percent. France grew 2 percent, supported by seaside stores and loyal local customers.

Asia excluding Japan increased 2 percent, helped by South Korea, while Greater China was stable in a difficult economic environment. The Middle East was the only region to contract, with sales down 4 percent at constant exchange rates. That regional split keeps China and the wider Asian luxury market central to the investment case.

Executive Chairman Axel Dumas said Hermès continues to pursue profitable growth and remains confident in its long-term vision. His comments emphasize the group’s artisanal model and long-term positioning rather than a short-term change in strategy.

sum: Hermès International stock traded at EUR 1,337.50 on Lang & Schwarz at 12:12 CET on Wednesday, November 4, 2026, 2.10 percent above the Xetra close of Tuesday, November 3, at EUR 1,310.00. The move came as investors assessed a broader luxury-sector reset rather than a new company announcement.

An October analysis hosted by the International Association of Department Stores and attributed to Bloomberg said European luxury shares had fallen about 40 percent in 2026. The report said weak Chinese demand, higher interest rates and fading pricing power had delayed hopes for a sector recovery.

The analysis placed Hermès among the luxury groups trading near their lowest valuations in 12 years. It said the company's premium to the sector had narrowed from 100 percent to 22 percent over 18 months, highlighting how a slower growth outlook can affect even the industry's strongest brands.

The sector backdrop remains uneven. The MSCI Europe Textiles Apparel and Luxury Goods index was down 25 percent in 2026 and almost 40 percent from its record high, according to the analysis. Price increases across the industry are also expected to be the lowest since 2019, limiting a key source of sales and margin support.

Analysts cited in the report expect luxury demand to concentrate further among top-tier clients while middle-income spending weakens. That shift favors brands with strong customer relationships and scarce products, but it also raises the importance of retaining the highest-spending clientele as broader demand cools.

Views on the downturn remain divided. UBS considers the weakness cyclical and favors Richemont and Watches of Switzerland, while Morgan Stanley sees limited room for multiple expansion over the next 12 months. Berenberg describes China's difficulties as structural, whereas Goldman Sachs sees 2027 as a potential turning point for mid-single-digit organic growth.

For Hermès, the debate centers on whether its brand strength and supply discipline can preserve pricing power through a prolonged luxury slowdown. The narrowing valuation premium means investors may require clearer evidence of renewed growth before the shares regain their former relative standing.

Hermes Birkin bags built their reputation on rarity, but shifting resale demand is changing the conversation
sum: For years, owning a Hermes Birkin bag was about more than carrying an expensive handbag. Its limited availability made it a status symbol, while the prospect of selling it at a substantial profit turned it into an alternative investment for some buyers. That equation, however, is beginning to change.

London-based reseller Cai Baochun, who began selling Birkins online and through social media in 2020, has stopped stockpiling the bags as second-hand prices weaken. “I don’t want to lose money,” he told Reuters.

According to Reuters, the resale value of unworn Birkins has fallen by more than $6,000 from its 2022 peak, reflecting a market where increasing availability is putting pressure on the premium buyers once paid to secure the coveted handbags.

The change is particularly visible in the Birkin 25, one of the brand's sought-after models. Its unworn black version now sells for around £24,000 on the resale market, according to luxury reseller Antoinette Hunter, founder of Lilac Blue.
That is approximately £4,000 below its 2022 price. Cai puts his asking price for the bag at around £20,000, while the same model retails for £9,390 in Britain, Reuters reported.

The Birkin, named after the late British-French actor Jane Birkin, has long been central to Hermès' luxury positioning. Access to the bag has often been linked to a customer's wider spending at the brand, including purchases of scarves, clothing and shoes.
Six resellers told Reuters that this practice remains common, although arrangements vary by region and store.

sum: European luxury stocks are plunging as weak consumer spending in China, the war in the Middle East, and protests in major European countries converge. Shares of French luxury group Kering, which owns Gucci, plunged 16% in a single day, while Hermès and LVMH also continued to fall.

According to Bloomberg and the Financial Times (FT), among other outlets, Kering shares plunged 16% on Oct. 23 (local time) on the Paris stock exchange, compared with the previous trading day. The decline followed the company's third-quarter results for this year, announced the previous day, which fell short of market expectations.
Gucci, Kering's flagship brand, posted a 6% year-on-year decline in third-quarter revenue. By contrast, retail sales at brands other than Gucci, including Saint Laurent and Bottega Veneta, rose 2%.

Kering said it would accelerate the closure of underperforming stores to improve its results. Armelle Poulou, Kering's chief financial officer (CFO), said the company had closed 105 stores so far and planned to close 20 more by the end of the year.

Other luxury companies are facing a similar situation. LVMH shares fell 1.5% on the day. According to Bloomberg, LVMH's forward price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio has fallen to about 16 times, its lowest level in more than a decade.

Hermès shares also fell 4%, reaching their lowest level in four years. Although the company had maintained relatively resilient results compared with other luxury groups, weakening demand in China meant it posted its slowest growth since 2020 in the third quarter of this year.

Hermès' forward P/E ratio is about 27 times, well below its post-COVID-19 pandemic peak of 70 times. German investment bank Berenberg downgraded its investment recommendation for Hermès from "Buy" to "Hold."

sum: Stocks for some of Europe’s most famous luxury brands are plummeting to their lowest level in years as Chinese customers cut back purchases and an industry revamp fails to launch.

Shares are down a jaw-dropping 40% so far this year for the continent’s fashion stalwarts — LVMH, parent company of Louis Vuitton, Christian Dior and more; Kering, which owns brands including Gucci and Bottega Veneta; and independent-minded Hermès.
“We know we have a lot of work to do in China,” the conglomerate’s finance chief Armelle Poulou said on an earnings call.
Kering sales dropped 1% in the third quarter. LVMH and Hermès each saw a 2% decrease. At Gucci alone, sales were down 6%.

The drop comes as the Chinese economy has been taken a beating. While unemployment is up, property values and household spending have been trending downward, according to the Journal. The country recently saw its slowest GDP growth since 2022.

“Despite the recent share price weakness, we expect some further pressure on the space as a whole today, with confirmation that the Chinese cluster seems to have taken a material (and bigger than feared) step down,” said JP Morgan analysts said in a note to investors about LVMH, according to Reuters.

The stock decline has put a dent in LVMH kingpin Bernard Arnault’s fortune. He last topped Forbes’ list of billionaires in 2024, when he was worth $233 billion, but his wealth is listed at around $171 billion today, putting him in seventh place.

sum: The aura of scarcity that has long surrounded Hermès's iconic Birkin bag is starting to loosen. A surge in secondary-market supply and a marked narrowing of resale premiums are casting the first systematic doubt on the core logic that has underpinned the brand's high valuation and fat margins over the past decade.

Of nine Birkin resellers interviewed by Reuters in the United States, Europe and Asia, six said secondhand prices had fallen over the past year, mainly because more bags are circulating in the market; five reported weakening demand. UBS analysts downgraded Hermès shares to "sell" earlier this month, estimating that the number of Birkins and Kellys currently listed for sale worldwide is six to seven times pre-pandemic levels, and said flatly that "we believe the nature of this business is changing."

Hermès shares have fallen nearly 40% so far this year, the worst performance among listed luxury companies. The company is due to report quarterly sales on Thursday, and consensus estimates compiled by Visible Alpha point to revenue growth of about 5.2%, which would be the slowest in six years.

The resale market for Birkins is cooling rapidly from its pandemic peak. Broker Bernstein, after tracking auction results, said the average resale price of a Birkin 25 in the third quarter of this year was about 1.7 times retail, well below the roughly 2.6 times seen at the 2022 peak.

Take the most sought-after unused black Birkin 25: resellers said its secondhand price has fallen by about £4,000 (approximately $5,400) since 2022 and now stands at about £24,000 (approximately $32,000), with some sellers asking as little as £20,000 (approximately $27,000). Hermès's official retail price in the UK is £9,390 (approximately $13,000) — the gap remains wide, but it is no longer what it once was.

Tsai Pao-chun, who runs a Birkin resale business in London, told Reuters he began selling through Vestiaire Collective and social media platforms in 2020, when resale prices could reach more than double retail and profits were rich. Today, unused Birkins sell for more than $6,000 below their 2022 peak, and he has stopped stockpiling. "I don't want to lose money," he said.

European Luxury Stocks Show Signs of Bottoming Out? Analysts Say Recovery Will Be Gradual, Not Linear — LVMH's 25% Discount Makes It a Value Play
sum: Holding European luxury stocks has become something of a contrarian trade these days, but signals that both consumer confidence and corporate earnings growth are bottoming out are giving this battered sector room to breathe. Analysts believe luxury stocks could see better performance over the next 12 months, though the recovery path will be gradual rather than a straight-line rebound.

European luxury stocks lagged the broader market by as much as 25% through May before beginning to stabilize. However, previous rallies have proven short-lived, and these stocks remain in laggard territory. The long-awaited sales recovery has failed to materialize, keeping the broader consumer discretionary complex subdued, with consumer sentiment equally depressed. China's stimulus measures have failed to ignite a recovery in either domestic or international markets, and the aftermath of the Iran conflict continues to cast a shadow over the sector.

Still, a team of JPMorgan strategists led by Mislav Matejka points out: "Interestingly, when consumer confidence is at depressed levels — as has been the case recently — consumer sectors tend to outperform over the following 12 months." They note that luxury is typically among the best-performing industries in such scenarios. "From a big-picture perspective, cyclical consumer sectors remain in the eye of the storm, facing earnings warnings and cautious guidance, but they could see better performance ahead."

The strategists note that after the University of Michigan Consumer Sentiment Index bottoms out, European luxury has historically outperformed the broader market by 9% to 12% on average. This view is built on the foundation of a potential future wealth effect. They argue that South Korea is emerging as a new growth engine, with retail sales so strong that the Korean market's importance now exceeds that of the Middle East. Meanwhile, as the macroeconomic environment stabilizes, Chinese demand should also begin to improve.

Earnings growth has been subdued for roughly two years, particularly relative to the broader market. However, signs are finally emerging that the worst may be over, with earnings expectations now pointing toward a growth inflection.

Meanwhile, shares of LVMH, the French industry heavyweight, nudged up about 1% following a muted earnings release earlier in the week. Other luxury names like Moncler ticked higher, while Richemont edged lower amid the choppy sector environment.

This patchwork of results suggests the luxury sector remains in a state of flux, with brand-specific narratives driving performance more so than broad-based momentum. sum: Investing.com -- Luxury goods maker Hermès International remains well positioned for long-term growth despite a disappointing start to 2026, with investors likely to focus on signs of improving momentum when the company reports second-quarter results on July 29, according to Jefferies.

The brokerage reiterated its Buy rating on the stock but lowered its price target to €2,000 from €2,400, citing continued mixed trends in China and a weaker-than-expected first quarter that shook confidence in the group's ability to sustain its industry-leading growth and profitability.

Jefferies said first-quarter organic sales growth of 5.6% surprised investors, with wholesale weakness, softer Middle East travel spending in Paris and sluggish Chinese demand weighing on performance. While the Americas posted strong 17.2% growth and Japan and Europe remained healthy, Asia excluding Japan grew just 2.2%, reflecting ongoing challenges in China.

For the second quarter, the broker expects organic revenue growth of 6.9%, slightly below market expectations of 7.3%, driven by 11% growth in leather goods and 3.5% growth in non-leather categories. It forecasts first-half EBIT of about €3.29 billion, broadly in line with consensus.

Jefferies noted several encouraging indicators ahead of the earnings release. The firm said Chinese quota spending for sought-after handbags appears to be recovering, Birkin auction premiums have improved globally, U.S. Google search interest in the brand has surged about 50% year-over-year in the second quarter, and global web traffic is running roughly 16% higher.

The brokerage argued the stock's valuation has become more attractive after a sharp derating. Shares now trade at around 33 times expected 2027 earnings, a significant discount to historical premium levels, suggesting investors are pricing in a prolonged slowdown in growth and returns.

The tentative diplomatic framework, which outlines the lifting of U.S. oil sanctions and the guaranteed reopening of the blockaded Strait of Hormuz, triggered an immediate risk-on rotation across continental trading floors.

Shares in high-end design houses LVMH, Kering, and Hermès skyrocketed by roughly 5%, leading a broader market rally that pushed the pan-European STOXX 600 index up 1.8% to reverse weeks of energy-driven stagflation fears.

The economic relief was immediate. While President Donald Trump later tempered the market enthusiasm via social media by stating that the accord was subject to the finalization of official documents, reports confirm that senior diplomats are on track to sign the treaty ahead of the upcoming Group of Seven leaders' summit.

The luxury sector emerged as the primary beneficiary of this geopolitical de-escalation. Hermès Madison Ave Window Art by Jeremy Olson Transforms Space
sum: At Hermès Madison Avenue, Jeremy Olson turns the storefront window into a passageway between worlds, where polished interiors buckle, bodies vanish into furniture and the logic of domestic space quietly begins to unravel. The Brooklyn-based artist has built a practice around the moment the familiar room stops obeying itself, when a sofa, curtain or ceiling becomes less a boundary than an invitation to cross into stranger weather.

The scene begins with a body disappearing into the upholstered depths of a couch, only to reappear elsewhere, slipping through drapery in a room turned upside down. The narrative folds in on itself again when an arm sinks into a bowl of pale liquid and emerges through the ceiling of the original interior, clutching a glowing globe. Its cord snakes through the composition like a trail of evidence, grounding the surreal sequence in something strangely tangible.

Olson’s wit lies in how little he needs to rupture reality. Yet enlarged beyond their proportions and bordered by mirrors, they become unstable, theatrical and faintly menacing. The storefront no longer behaves as display, but as a threshold.
Step close, and the ordinary begins to split open. Olson invites us to look past the glass and accept another grammar of space without resistance. 706 Madison Ave

items.t: 4 Takeaways From Luxury’s Q1 Earnings
sum: Luxury’s hopes for a slight first-quarter rebound have been set back, as conflict in the Middle East delivers a blow to performance.

“Q1 didn’t really change the sector’s outlook, and, if anything, it slowed down or pushed back the recovery story we had in mind,” Barclays head of European luxury goods research Carole Madjo says. “The market has lowered its Q2 estimates to factor in the impact of the Middle East conflict and the disrupted tourism environment. The sector’s downgrade cycle is still ongoing on the top line, and potentially on margins as well.”
HSBC anticipated a 5.5% increase in global luxury sales in Q1 2026. However, the average organic sales growth of LVMH, Kering, Hermès, Moncler, and Prada materialized at 4.2%.

“For most companies, momentum in China is improving every quarter. The big issue continues to be the drop in Chinese tourism,” TD Cowen analyst Oliver Chen says. “The US continues to be a resilient and attractive market, with a K-shaped economy — where the top end grows, but the lower end is seeing more pressure particularly as consumers watch gas prices. The strongest momentum comes from jewelry.”

While soft luxury brands have shown relative weakness, the jewelry “supercycle” continues. Sales at LVMH’s watches and jewelry division, Kering’s jewelry arm, and Hermès jewelry were up 7%, 22%, and almost 10%, respectively. This bodes well for Cartier owner Richemont, which will publish its annual earnings on May 22.

At LVMH’s annual general meeting on April 23, chair and CEO Bernard Arnault warned investors that the Middle East crisis “could turn into a global catastrophe with extremely serious and very negative economic consequences”. He added: “In which case, who can say how 2026 will play out? Or it might be resolved one way or another more quickly, which is what we all hope for, even if it doesn’t seem easy; and in that case, business will gradually return to normal.”
Despite variation between companies, the conflict in the Middle East has impacted sales growth by around 1 to 2 percentage points.

items.t: Luxury stocks slide – should you buy dip in the luxuries sector?
sum: Shares in luxury goods giant Hermès (PA:RMS) tanked on 15 April following warnings of a sales slowdown in its key market. But despite the luxury sector facing obvious challenges, some analysts think that there is a buying opportunity for bargain-priced luxury stocks, especially if you can spot the hidden gems.

March was a choppy month for the stock market, with the direction of travel made clear by investors’ buying trends. As the Iran war shook global outlooks, investors bought up defence and energy stocks, and went cautious in a bid to protect portfolios from volatility and profit from higher oil prices.

Hermès shares fell 8% on Wednesday, having been down more than 14% at one point in the day. The Middle East region had been the company’s fastest-growing market, but quarterly sales in the region fell 6% in constant exchange rate from the same period a year prior.

“Sales in the Middle East have, unsurprisingly, been most affected, but so too have sales in China – one of the luxury sector’s most important regions,” said Emma Wall, chief investment strategist at investment platform Hargreaves Lansdown. “Hermès also revealed sales in Paris are down, as fewer shoppers undertake international travel.”
Since the start of the conflict in Iran, Hermès shares are down 25%.

LVMH (PA:MC) – which owns the iconic Moët & Chandon, Hennessy and Louis Vuitton brands – saw its share price fall as much as 2.7% on Wednesday, though they recovered most of these losses later in the day. But LVMH shares too are down 14% since the start of the conflict.
There is clearly pressure on luxury stocks, but do the recent falls constitute a buying opportunity?

Louis Vuitton, Gucci, Hermès luxury sales decline as Iran war hits crucial Middle East demand
sum: The US-Israeli war with Iran is having knock-on effects everywhere, including energy markets, materials, and travel. One typically immune sector is also getting hit hard: luxury.

The war, which started in late February, has put a big dent in the $400 billion luxury goods sector. All the big luxury houses are suffering losses from the growing and high-spending Middle East markets, the lucrative travel and aspirational clients who spend heavily on vacations, and, of course, increased costs due to logistics and materials.
It all started with LVMH (MC.PA), the world's largest luxury conglomerate behind brands like Louis Vuitton, Christian Dior, Loewe, Bulgari, and Tiffany & Co.
LVMH reported Q1 revenue of 19.1 billion euros, a 6% decline, missing analyst expectations of a 1.5% increase, reflecting the toll of the war.

"The quarter was impacted by the ongoing conflict in Middle East, which had a tangible incidence on demand in the region in March after a good start of the year, and this accounting for a negative one percentage point on the growth of the quarter. So excluding this impact, organic growth would have been plus 2%," CFO Cécile Cabanis said on the earnings call on Monday.
Fashion and leather goods (-9%), perfumes and cosmetics (-6%), followed by selective retailing (Sephora, DFS travel retail, and Le Bon Marché department stores), took the biggest hits.
Kering (KER.PA), behind brands like Gucci, Bottega Veneta, and Balenciaga, also felt the impact.

It seems that even Hermès’ scarcity model is beginning to falter
sum: Even Hermès is faltering. Analysts are concerned because the luxury house’s scarcity model, which has always produced fewer products than demand, appears to be showing signs of strain. Why? It’s failing to win over younger generations, who are redefining the boundaries of luxury, while accusations of unfair business practices are tarnishing the house’s prestige. Some evidence of this, observers note, can be seen in the second-hand market, where the price of Birkin and Kelly bags has fallen.

Over the past three years, Hermès’ revenue has risen by 38%, while LVMH’s has increased by 2% and Kering’s has fallen by 28%. Hermès shares are trading at over 45 times earnings, compared to 23 times for LVMH. This is to make it clear that we are not talking about a brand in crisis, but one that may stop growing as it has in the past. “One Bag Too Many” is the evocative title of the report by UBS analyst Zuzanna Pusz, who downgraded Hermès stock last year from “outperform” to “neutral”.

“We are increasingly concerned that this new scale, especially in the leather goods’ sector”, reads the excerpt from Business of Fashion, “could make the brand potentially more ubiquitous and, in the long term, more cyclical”. Today, it’s no longer as rare as it once was to see Hermès products on the street (and on social media). The fashion house seems a bit less exclusive. This is evident in UBS surveys in China. In the 2024 edition of the study, 29% of the sample cited Hermès among their favorite brands; that figure dropped to 22% in 2025.

Another sign of weakness comes from the resale market. According to a Bernstein study dated February 16, in the fourth quarter of 2025, the average resale prices of Birkin and Kelly bags were 1.4 times higher than the retail price of new items in stores. This ratio is down from 2021 and 2022, when it stood at 2x. Lawsuits over alleged unfair business practices have tarnished the brand’s prestige, as we mentioned. For younger generations, owning a Birkin means submitting to Hermès and playing by its rules.
The risk is that the public will talk less about the brand’s narrative, its cultural values, and product quality, and more about the cost required to access it, notes Ladymax.

items.t: Victoria Beckham Totes a $50,980 Hermès Kelly to Paris Fashion Week
sum: Ugg slippers are a pre- and post-Paris Fashion Week essential in Gigi Hadid, Elsa Hosk, and Lily Rose-Depp's survival kits. Victoria Beckham, on the other hand, only prefers suede and shearling on rare Hermès bags. For instance, she traded Tasmans for a fluffy Hermès Kelly bag on March 2, the first day of Paris Fashion Week.

Four days before her Fall 2026 runway show, the creative director was spotted on the streets of Paris wearing one of her favorite color combinations. On top, a tomato red turtleneck endorsed a leading Spring 2026 shade, which she tucked into ultra-high-rise, khaki trousers. In true Beckham fashion, each wide-leg hem stretched so long, her choice of footwear remained a mystery. However, Marie Claire instantly recognized her bundled-up Kelly as the collector's item Mouton model.
Hermès's Fauve Doblis Suede—as seen on Beckham's latest Kelly bag—hardly ever materializes on the designer's arm. The reason? It's actually discontinued.

Beckham's Kelly first debuted on the Fall 2005 runway by then-creative director Jean Paul Gaultier, alongside matching winterwear. Mouton shearling trim lined the bag's short handle, the top-flap, and every outer edge, just like the insoles of a cozy winter boot. Extremely rare, dark brown leather called Ebene Barenia bookended the closure's palladium hardware, as well as the elongated crossbody strap. Every element looked good as new on Beckham, despite the bag being a 21-year-old piece in her Hermès stock. (She first wore it in early 2006.)
The Kelly's discontinued suede and slipper-like shearling make it one of the priciest purses in Beckham's closet. Today, it sells secondhand for upwards of $50,980.

Beckham's Kelly Mouton hasn't been publicly photographed in over a decade, but her red-and-khaki set mirrored a more recent look. Posh Spice wore an almost-identical turtleneck and trousers from her own label to her London flagship store in November. Her Hermes Kellys earned the day off in favor of her label's $1,090 Dorian Pochette Top-Handle Bag. Its Burgundy tint was a few shades deeper than her tomato-y top, similar to the croc-embossed Birkin she carried on Jan. 27.
Beckham's shearling-trimmed Kelly is the closest she's come to wearing Uggs in a decade.

sum: Hermès International (FR0000125452) entered the September 1, 2026 session with its stock supported by a resilient first-half 2026 margin profile and a market capitalization in the upper tier of global luxury, even as revenue growth cooled compared with prior years. Per a consolidated overview published for the first half of 2026, group revenue reached 8,163 million EUR in the six months to June 30, 2026, while the operating margin held at 41.0 percent, underlining the brand's pricing power and cost discipline. A recent market snapshot dated August 31, 2026 placed the shares at 1,598 EUR on Euronext Paris, leaving the valuation premium intact against peers as investors weigh slower top-line growth against consistently high profitability.

The latest published key figures for Hermès show that in the first half of 2026 the group generated 8,163 million EUR in revenue, compared with 8,034 million EUR in the first half of 2025, which corresponds to reported growth of 1.6 percent year over year and 6.1 percent at constant exchange rates. The same overview indicates that current operating income for the first half of 2026 came to 3,351 million EUR, marginally above the 3,327 million EUR recorded in the first half of 2025, with the current operating margin steady at 41.0 percent versus 41.4 percent a year earlier. Net profit attributable to the group for the first half of 2026 was 2,238 million EUR, while the net margin stood at 27.4 percent of sales, reflecting a business that is still highly profitable despite a softer pace of revenue expansion. After adjusting for the exceptional contribution on the profits of large French companies, management reports that the net margin in the first half of 2026 would have stood at 30.7 percent, versus 31.2 percent in the first half of 2025 and 30.3 percent for full-year 2025, signalling only a slight compression in underlying profitability.

The key figures table for the period also highlights Hermès' cash generation and balance sheet strength. Adjusted free cash flow reached 2,182 million EUR in the first half of 2026, up from 1,847 million EUR in the first half of 2025, showing that cash creation increased by 335 million EUR year on year even as revenue growth slowed.
